How to reduce a photo to 20 KB

Get a photo down to 20 KB for an exam form without turning it into a blurry mess, and avoid the mistake that makes portals reject it anyway.

What actually controls file size

Three things decide how many kilobytes a JPG takes up: how many pixels it contains, how much detail sits in those pixels, and how hard the JPEG encoder is told to squeeze. Most people only ever touch the first one, shrinking the image until the number falls, and end up with something too small to be accepted.

The second factor is the one nobody thinks about. A photograph taken against a plain white wall compresses far smaller than the same photograph taken in front of a bookshelf, at identical dimensions and identical quality. JPEG stores difference between neighbouring pixels, and a flat background has almost none to store. If you are struggling to hit a tight limit, reshooting against a blank wall will do more than any slider.

The mistake that gets photos rejected

Almost every form asks for a range rather than a ceiling. Twenty to fifty kilobytes. Ten to twenty. Four to thirty. People read the upper number, compress as hard as their tool allows, and submit a 6 KB file against a 20 KB minimum.

That file is rejected exactly as firmly as one that came in at 200 KB, and the error message usually says nothing more helpful than that the upload failed. If your photo keeps bouncing and you have been making it smaller each time, you are very likely walking further away from the answer with every attempt.

Check the minimum in your notification before you compress anything. If it says 20 to 50 KB, aim for the middle, around 35 KB, so small variations do not push you outside the range.

Doing it without losing quality

Set the pixel dimensions first, exactly as the form specifies. Only then adjust compression. Doing it the other way round means compressing twice, and JPEG loses a little detail every single time it is re-encoded, which is why a photo forwarded through three WhatsApp chats looks soft.

Always work from the original file out of your camera roll, not from a copy that has already been sent somewhere. Messaging apps compress on send. The version your friend sent back to you has already lost detail you cannot recover.

If you must lose something, lose it from the background rather than the face. Cropping tighter reduces pixel count and file size at once, without touching the quality of what remains.

When 20 KB is genuinely hard

The trouble is not the target, it is the target combined with the dimensions. Twenty kilobytes is comfortable for a 140 by 60 signature and cramped for a 400 by 500 photograph, because the second one has to spread the same budget across twenty times as many pixels.

If your form asks for large dimensions and a small file, expect some quality loss and plan around it. Shoot in good light, against a plain background, with the subject filling the frame. A sharp, well lit photo survives heavy compression. A dim one taken in a hurry falls apart.

Padding, and why it is not cheating

Sometimes an image compresses well below the minimum even at the highest quality setting, particularly small signatures on white paper where there is almost nothing to encode. You cannot make the file bigger by adding quality that is not there.

The standard fix is a JPEG comment segment. The format allows blocks of arbitrary data that every decoder skips over, so the file gets heavier while the image stays pixel for pixel identical. The portal reads a file inside its accepted range and displays exactly the image you saw. Our resizer does this automatically when it needs to, and tells you when it has.
